articles.title: Eye on Everything
articles.summary: This article outlines several upcoming events for the club, including a July general meeting with Bob Garfinkle on Lunar Nomenclature, a Yosemite/Glacier Point star party, and the AANC annual star-b-q. It also calls for members to join the SJAA's Observatory Committee, which has $6,500 for site acquisition and construction, and thanks individuals for their help with newsletter publishing.

articles.title: Activities Calendar
articles.summary: The article presents an activities calendar for June, July, and August, detailing various astronomical events, club meetings, and educational opportunities. Highlights include multiple star parties at different state parks and Houge Park, general meetings featuring speakers like Bob Garfinkle on Lunar Nomenclature, and observational astronomy classes. The calendar also notes board meetings, club-specific star parties at Yosemite and Mt. Lassen, and provides contact information.

articles.title: Texas Star Party
articles.summary: The author attended the Texas Star Party (TSP) from May 11th-18th at Prude Ranch near McDonald Observatory, describing it as an "awesome" experience despite hot, dusty days. The nights offered incredible views of deep-sky objects, with the Milky Way appearing like cumulus clouds and detailed observations of numerous galaxies. The event hosted over 700 attendees and nearly as many telescopes, creating an impressive observing environment.

articles.title: RTMC: Reflections From a SnowFlake
articles.summary: The author reflects on their first RTMC (Riverside Telescope Makers Conference) experience, describing it as a memorable event despite unexpected snowfall. They highlight the joy of children and adults viewing celestial objects once the skies cleared, and express deep gratitude for the organizers, staff, and volunteers whose efforts made the conference a resounding success, including excellent meal services. The author looks forward to attending future RTMC events.

articles.title: JOB, PEOPLE!
articles.summary: This article offers a personal and enthusiastic thank-you note reflecting on a successful astronomy event, praising the vendors, engaging speakers, and fellow astronomy enthusiasts, including IRC participants. The author emphasizes the vibrant community, the stimulating knowledge shared, and the overall enjoyment of the experience, despite not covering specific astronomy angles.

articles.title: Houge Park Star Party, May 24
articles.summary: A star party at Houge Park on May 24, attended by over 100 people and 15 telescopes, started with promising clear skies for viewing the Moon, Venus, and various deep-sky objects. However, the event was abruptly cut short around 9:30 PM when the park sprinklers unexpectedly turned on, scattering the public and forcing many participants to relocate their equipment. Despite the incident, some dedicated observers continued viewing from the parking lot and sidewalks under the transparent sky until late.

articles.title: TSP, continued from page 1
articles.summary: The author recounts a highly successful experience at the Texas Star Party (TSP), praising the exceptionally dark skies that enabled naked-eye viewing of faint stars and challenging telescopic observations like Pluto, significantly enhancing views of nebulae with O-III filters. The event also featured promising observations of Comet Hale-Bopp, the introduction of new astronomical gear, and a strong sense of camaraderie among attendees despite environmental challenges. Overall, TSP was a memorable and rewarding experience that combined outstanding stargazing with unique social and regional exploration.

articles.title: In Memory of Tom Waineo
articles.summary: Tom Waineo, a professional optician, mentor to amateur telescope makers (ATMs), and optics writer, passed away suddenly at the age of 60 in Bradenton, Florida. He was recently retired and known for his generosity with time and contributions to the optics and amateur astronomy communities, and will be greatly missed.

articles.title: Texas Star Party
articles.summary: Brian Skiff recounts his experience at the Texas Star Party (TSP) in May, detailing variable observing conditions, including two clear nights, and numerous deep-sky observations made with various large telescopes. He highlights significant sightings like faint planetary nebulae, globular clusters, an asteroid, and an x-ray nova, often observed for the first time by attendees. The report also covers talks by notable astronomers and critically assesses the optical quality of many large telescopes at the event, while praising a few specific instruments.

articles.title: Back Yard Astronomy
articles.summary: Mark Wagner recounts a pleasant June evening of backyard astronomy with his children in Los Gatos, CA, using a 10-inch f/5.6 Dobsonian telescope. Despite in-town light pollution, they enjoyed observing various celestial objects, including prominent globular clusters like M13 and M3, galaxies such as M51 and M63, and planetary nebulae. The report highlights the joy of sharing the hobby with family and the rewards of urban observing.

articles.title: Periodical Publication Statement
articles.summary: The SJAA Ephemeris, the official newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association, is published monthly throughout the year, from January to December. The statement also provides the mailing address for the San Jose Astronomical Association.

articles.title: T2, continued from page 4
articles.summary: This article snippet highlights the ongoing shift towards technology in astronomical observing, noting the prevalent use of 486 laptops with MegaStar software instead of paper charts. It anticipates future enhancements like Ethernet access on observing fields, enabling astronomers to use web-based tools such as SkyView, NED, and SIMBAD, thus ushering in a 'paperless observing' era.

articles.title: Lunar Prospector Spacecraft Construction
articles.summary: Construction and assembly of the Lunar Prospector spacecraft are on schedule for an October 1997 launch, marking the first competitively selected mission in NASA's 'faster, better, cheaper' Discovery series. The article details its innovative management style, focusing on minimizing risk and cost with rapid decision-making, and outlines its scientific objectives, including mapping lunar composition, gravity, magnetic fields, and searching for polar water ice. The spacecraft, a small, spin-stabilized vehicle, will conduct a one-year polar orbiting mission to gather crucial data for future lunar exploration.

articles.title: Early Findings from Tethered Satellite Mission Point to Revamping of Space Physics Theories
articles.summary: Data from the Tethered Satellite System Reflight (TSS-1R) mission on Space Shuttle Columbia's STS-75 has revealed early findings that are challenging and revising long-standing space physics and plasma theories. The mission observed tether currents up to three times greater than predicted, indicating significant potential for future technological applications like power generation and propulsion. Additionally, new insights were gained into thruster-ionosphere interactions and the characteristics of high-voltage plasma sheaths in orbit, which were previously difficult to study.

articles.title: Temperature in Space
articles.summary: Temperature in space is a complex concept: while a perfect vacuum lacks temperature, real space contains sparse, high-temperature particles with low heat density. Large objects achieve an equilibrium temperature based on heat input from stars/planets and output via blackbody radiation, influenced by factors like albedo and geometry. The Cosmic Microwave Background radiation ultimately establishes a universal minimum temperature of approximately 3 Kelvin for all natural objects in space.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: This article, 'COMET COMMENTS' by Don Machholz, provides an update on Comet Hale-Bopp (C/1995 O1), noting its current naked-eye visibility for some and projected long-term visibility until mid-May 1997 in the Northern Hemisphere. It encourages readers to track the comet's unaided visibility duration as a personal record. The piece also mentions Periodic Comet Kopff (22P/Kopff) is visible with optical aid and includes detailed ephemeris data for both comets.

articles.title: Orbital Elements
articles.summary: This document presents a table detailing the orbital elements for two celestial objects: Comet Hale-Bopp and Comet Kopff. It provides specific data points such as perihelion date and distance, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, and orbital period for each comet. The information appears to be technical data derived from sources like the Minor Planet Center (MPC).

articles.title: Celestial Calendar - July 1996
articles.summary: This article, 'Celestial Calendar - July 1996', provides a detailed astronomical guide for the month. It includes tables for lunar phases, the positions and observational data for Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, as well as solar information (SOL). Additionally, it specifies astronomical twilight times, sidereal time, and highlights the 'Darkest Saturday Night' on July 13th.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Program Status
articles.summary: This document provides a status update for a telescope loaner program, listing various telescopes available for borrowing by members. It details each scope's description, current borrower, due date, and whether it is currently available. Interested members are directed to contact Paul Barton to utilize the program.

articles.title: Pioneer 10 & 11 Status Reports
articles.summary: This report details the status of the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft as of May 1996. Pioneer 10 remains healthy and operational, continuing to send scientific observations from the outer Solar System, although its Cosmic Ray Telescope was recently deactivated due to power constraints, and it will undergo superior conjunction in early June. Pioneer 11's mission has concluded, with its last communication in November 1995 due to an exhausted power source.

articles.title: Astro Ads
articles.summary: This document is a classifieds section titled "Astro Ads," featuring several used astronomical items for sale, including a Meade 12.5" Starfinder Dobsonian, an Astro-Physics 155mm f9 EDT APO, and an Orion 12.5" Premium Reflector. Each listing provides details, condition, price, and contact information for the seller. The section also states that these ads are free for noncommercial advertisers selling astronomically related products or services.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document from July 1996 outlines the Officers and Board of Directors for an organization, listing positions such as President, VP, Treasurer, Secretary, and multiple Directors. It provides contact phone numbers for these individuals, as well as for Ephemeris Contributors and the Editor.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing membership types (standard and junior) and associated fees, with an option to add a Sky & Telescope subscription. It provides instructions for submitting the form and payment via mail or in person at an SJAA meeting, along with contact information for the treasurer. The form also includes an address for the non-profit organization.
